answers.T4_traffic: With nothing cached, the naive inner loop moves 16 B per 2 flops, about 16·N³/6 = 2.86 GB for N = 1024, which at 1.58 s is only 1.8 GB/s of effective bandwidth. The left-looking loop streams one column (8 B per 2 flops) while column j stays in cache, so it moves half the data with stride 1, and it ran 40.7x faster.
answers.T1_dependencies: Row i of the baseline needs all earlier rows of L through long dot products, so the rows form one chain of dependent computations. In the right-looking form, once column j is final, every trailing column update A[:,k] -= A[:,j]·A[k,j] touches different data, so the columns can be updated independently by different threads.
answers.BONUS: Option A: cholesky_dag! removes the phase barriers; each tile task waits only for the tasks that last wrote the tiles it uses, and it ran in 0.00651 s versus 0.00668 s for the fork-join version. Option C: cholesky_recursive! splits the matrix in halves (POTRF, TRSM, SYRK, POTRF) with a 64-column loop leaf, and ran in 0.0056 s against 0.014 s for LAPACK. All variants pass the backward-error test.
answers.T8_recommendation: Deploy tiled_blas in Float64: at N = 4096 it takes 0.133 s (172.4 GFlop/s) with backward error 1.8e-15, well below 10·N·ε. It is the fastest measured option at this size and passes the backward-error test; mixed-precision IR with a Float32 LAPACK factor is the next step if N grows.
answers.T7_ai_derivation: Naive: 2 flops per 16 B of loads = 0.125 flop/B. Left-looking: 2 flops per 8 B of the streamed column (column j stays in cache) = 0.25 flop/B. Tiled, tiled_blas and lapack: a tile GEMM does 2nb³ flops on 3nb²·8 B, i.e. nb/12 flop/B, with nb = 64 for tiled and nb = 128 for the BLAS versions. The theoretical peak is cores × GHz × SIMD lanes × 2 (FMA) × FMA units = 6 × 4.5 × 4 × 2 × 2 = 432.0 GFlop/s.
answers.T6_methodology: Each run starts with a warm-up call that excludes JIT compilation, and the minimum of 3 repetitions on a fresh copy of the matrix is reported. The exponent fit uses the four largest available sizes per implementation (three for naive, which is capped at NAIVE_MAX_N). Thread counts are fixed (8 Julia threads, 8 BLAS threads), only the factorization is timed, and every result is validated with the backward error.
answers.T1_scaling: At p = 8 the speed-up is 2.31x (efficiency 0.29) against an ideal of 8x. Scaling stops because every column ends with an @sync barrier after a short update, the diagonal and scaling steps stay serial (fitted f = 0.454, so S ≤ 1/f), and the update is limited by memory bandwidth.
answers.T4_cache: Three nb × nb Float64 tiles fit in a 512 KiB L2 cache for nb ≤ 147 (128 as a power of two), while the measured best was nb = 64. The best nb is also set by task count and load balance across threads, not only by cache capacity.
answers.T7_interpretation: The ridge point is 6.83 flop/B. lapack is compute-bound at 51.9% of its roof; left is memory-bound at 40.9% of its roof; naive is memory-bound at 5.0% of its roof; tiled is memory-bound at 21.3% of its roof; tiled_blas is compute-bound at 69.4% of its roof. A fraction above 100% means the traffic model overestimates memory traffic because data is reused from cache. Memory-bound versions move up by reusing data in cache (blocking, larger tiles), compute-bound ones by better SIMD/FMA kernels and more cores.
answers.T8_conclusions:
- Task granularity matters: the tiled version runs at 2.96x the speed of the column-wise threaded one.
- Data movement mattered most for sequential code: the left-looking loop was 40.7x faster than the naive one.
- Float32 gave 0.92x, and mixed IR recovered Float64 accuracy in 3 steps.
- My best own code reaches 161.7% of LAPACK; register-blocked kernels would be the next step.
answers.T5_gap: My best own version reaches 161.7% of LAPACK's speed. OpenBLAS blocks for the cache levels, packs the operands, and uses register-blocked SIMD micro-kernels with FMA, whereas my tile loops reload data from cache on every update and are only auto-vectorized.
answers.T2_barriers: Each step k has two @sync barriers, one after the TRSM tasks and one after the update tasks, plus the sequential POTRF. A DAG scheduler could start POTRF(k+1) as soon as tile (k+1,k+1) is updated, and TRSM(i,k+1) right after it, without waiting for the other updates of step k.
answers.T5_oversubscription: Julia tasks that each call multi-threaded BLAS create more threads than cores, so they compete for the cores and the run slows down. cholesky_tiled_blas! sets BLAS to 1 thread, so only the tile tasks provide parallelism, and restores 8 threads in a finally block.
answers.T3_tradeoff: Float32 was 0.92x faster than Float64 (0.00819 s vs 0.00757 s). The backward error grew from 8.5e-16 to 2.4e-7 and the forward error from 3.3e-13 to 0.00011, i.e. about 8.5 digits were lost.
answers.T6_observations: The fastest implementation is tiled_blas at N = 256 and tiled_blas at N = 4096, where it reaches 172.4 GFlop/s. GFlop/s generally rises with N as fixed overheads (task spawning, barriers, BLAS startup) are amortized and cache reuse improves, and drops once the matrix no longer fits in cache. The naive baseline stays low because of its stride-N accesses, and the measured exponents (1.73 to 3.92) approach the ideal 3 only where the N³ work outweighs the overheads.
answers.T3_ir: The residual b − A·x is computed in Float64, so each cheap Float32 solve with the existing factor corrects the error and shrinks it by about κ(A)·ε₃₂ per step. Here it reached backward error 7.8e-16 in 3 steps. IR fails when κ(A)·ε₃₂ ≳ 1 (κ ≳ 10⁷), because the Float32 factor is then too inaccurate to contract the error.
answers.T2_granularity: At small nb there are many tiny tasks (357632 at nb = 8), so spawn and scheduling overhead and poor cache reuse dominate. At large nb there are only a few big tasks, so threads sit idle and the serial POTRF on a large tile lies on the critical path. The minimum at nb = 64 (47.94 GFlop/s) balances the two.
